title: Greetings, introductions and the vocative
objectives: I can greet people at different times of day and say goodbye, choosing the phrase that suits the time and the person.
I can introduce myself, ask someone's name and say that I am pleased to meet them.
I can say where I am from and what my nationality is, with the word for a man or for a woman.
I can address people with the vocative of their first name, with 'па́не' and 'па́ні', and with a first name and patronymic.
I can use 'дя́кую', 'будь ла́ска' and 'ви́бачте' and say what each one literally means.

vocabulary.note: The noun 'приві́т' means 'greeting', and on its own it is the everyday hello between people who say 'ти' to each other. It is only a hello, never a goodbye. To a stranger, an older person or a teacher, say 'до́брий день' instead.

'До́брий' is the adjective 'good', in the masculine form because 'день' (day) is a masculine noun. It is the standard greeting from late morning until evening, polite with anyone, and the safest choice with strangers and in shops and offices.
'Ра́нок' is the masculine noun for 'morning', so 'до́брий' is masculine here too. It is said early in the day; from late morning on, people say 'до́брий день'.
'Ве́чір' (evening) is masculine, like 'день' and 'ра́нок'. It is a hello for the evening only; to say goodbye in the evening, use 'до поба́чення' or 'бува́й'.

'На' is a preposition meaning 'on' or 'for', and 'добра́ніч' is one word made from 'до́бра' (good, feminine) and 'ніч' (night, a feminine noun). It wishes someone a good night's sleep, so it is said only when someone goes to bed, never as a greeting.

'До' is a preposition meaning 'until', and 'поба́чення' is a noun made from the verb 'поба́чити', 'to see', so the phrase means 'until we see each other again'. It is the neutral, polite goodbye, used with anyone. On its own, the word 'поба́чення' also means a date, a planned romantic meeting.

It is the imperative, the command form, of the verb 'бува́ти', which means 'to be' in the sense of being somewhere from time to time. It is short for 'бува́й здоро́в', 'be healthy'. Say it to one person you call 'ти'; to a person you call 'ви', or to a group, say 'бува́йте'. 'До за́втра', literally 'until tomorrow', is the goodbye for 'see you tomorrow'.
It is the 'я' form of the verb 'дя́кувати', 'to thank', so it says 'I thank'. It is used with anyone. 'Ду́же дя́кую' is 'thank you very much', and the usual reply is 'будь ла́ска'.

'Будь' is the imperative of 'бу́ти', 'to be', and 'ла́ска' is a feminine noun meaning 'kindness' or 'favor'. The phrase never changes, and it does three jobs: 'please' in a request, 'you're welcome' after thanks, and 'here you are' when you hand something to someone.

It is the imperative of 'ви́бачити', 'to forgive', in the form for a person you call 'ви' or for a group; to someone you call 'ти', say 'ви́бач'. It serves both to get a stranger's attention and to apologize.

example.source: Excuse me, what is your name?

vocabulary.note: 'Як' means 'how', and 'спра́ви' is the plural of 'спра́ва', 'affair' or 'matter'. The question has no verb. It is a friendly question between people who know each other, and the answer is usually short: 'до́бре', 'ду́же до́бре'.

It is the adverb made from 'до́брий', 'good', and it means 'well'. Where English answers 'How are you?' with 'good' or 'fine', Ukrainian answers with this adverb. It also says how something is done: 'Ти до́бре гово́риш.' is 'You speak well.'

'Ду́же' means 'very', and 'приє́мно' means 'pleasant'. 'Приє́мно' is a predicative word, which the note on greetings explains. Say the phrase when you meet someone for the first time, after you hear their name; the other person usually says it back.

example.source: Nice to meet you, Mr. Andrii.

vocabulary.note: 'Мене́' is the form of 'я' used for the object of a verb, English 'me', and 'зва́ти' is the infinitive 'to call'. The sentence has no subject: it says 'me to-call', in effect 'people call me'. The name after it stays in the nominative, its dictionary form.
It asks for the place someone or something comes from. 'Зві́дки ти?' and 'Зві́дки ви?' need no verb, and the answer uses 'з' with the place: 'Я з Кана́ди.'
Like other feminine nouns in '-а', it changes its ending after 'з': 'з Кана́ди', 'from Canada'.

A Ukrainian word for a nationality is a noun that names the person, one word for a man and another for a woman, and it is written with a small letter. In the other forms of this word the 'е' of the last syllable drops out: the plural, used for men or for a mixed group, is 'украї́нці'.
The word for a woman ends in '-ка'. It is also used for a girl.

example.source: Oksana is from Kyiv. She is Ukrainian.

vocabulary.note: It is built like 'украї́нець', with '-ець' for a man, and its 'е' also drops out in other forms: the plural is 'кана́дці'.
It is built like 'украї́нка', with '-ка' for a woman.

dialogues.title: Meeting at a university event
dialogues.context: At an evening event at the university in Kyiv, Oksana meets Sam, a Canadian who is learning Ukrainian. They are young, so they say 'ти' from the start. Then Oksana's friend Taras arrives.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: Nice to meet you, Sam. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я з Кана́ди. Я кана́дець. А ти?
lines.source: I'm from Canada. I'm Canadian. And you?
lines.source_literal: I from Canada. I Canadian-man. And you?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: Fine, thanks. Sam, this is Taras.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: Nice to meet you, Sam. Are you Ukrainian?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ні, я не украї́нець. Я кана́дець.
lines.source: No, I'm not Ukrainian. I'm Canadian.
lines.source_literal: No, I not Ukrainian-man. I Canadian-man.

dialogues.title: Meeting the teacher
dialogues.context: Before his first Ukrainian lesson, Sam looks for his teacher, Iryna Petrivna, in a university corridor. She is older than he is and she is his teacher, so he says 'ви' to her; she says 'ви' to him too, as teachers often do with adult students.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день! Ви́бачте, ви Іри́на Петрі́вна?
lines.source: Hello! Excuse me, are you Iryna Petrivna?
lines.source_literal: Good day! Forgive, you Iryna Petrivna?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, це я. До́брий день! Як вас зва́ти?
lines.source: Yes, that's me. Hello! What is your name?
lines.source_literal: Yes, this I. Good day! How you to-call?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мене́ зва́ти Сем. Ду́же приє́мно, па́ні Іри́но.
lines.source: My name is Sam. Nice to meet you, Ms. Iryna.
lines.source_literal: Me to-call Sam. Very pleasant, madam Iryna.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же приє́мно, Се́ме. Ви кана́дець, так?
lines.source: Nice to meet you, Sam. You're Canadian, right?
lines.source_literal: Very pleasant, Sam. You Canadian-man, yes?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, я з Кана́ди. А ви з Ки́єва?
lines.source: Yes, I'm from Canada. And are you from Kyiv?
lines.source_literal: Yes, I from Canada. And you from Kyiv?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, я з Ки́єва. Ви до́бре гово́рите!
lines.source: Yes, I'm from Kyiv. You speak well!
lines.source_literal: Yes, I from Kyiv. You well speak!

dialogues.title: Morning and evening at Andrii's café
dialogues.context: Andrii owns the café near Oksana's home. In the morning Halyna, Oksana's mother, comes in; she and Andrii say 'ви' and use 'па́не' and 'па́ні'. In the evening Taras drops by for a coffee and later says goodbye; he and Andrii, who are friends, say 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: До́брий ра́нок, па́не Андрі́ю! Як спра́ви?
lines.source: Good morning, Mr. Andrii! How are you?
lines.source_literal: Good morning, mister Andrii! How affairs?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре. Чай із цу́кром, будь ла́ска.
lines.source: Very well. Tea with sugar, please.
lines.source_literal: Very well. Tea with sugar, be kindness.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: Hi, Andrii! Is there any coffee?

grammar.title: The vocative: calling someone by name
grammar.explanation:
The vocative is the case of the person you are speaking to. Unit 5 listed it as the seventh case, 'кли́чний відмі́нок', the calling case. English shows that a name is being called only with a comma and the voice; Ukrainian also changes the ending of the name. Whenever you speak to someone by name, to greet them, thank them, ask them something or say goodbye, the name is in the vocative: 'Окса́но, приві́т!' When you speak about a person, or say who someone is, the name stays in the nominative, its dictionary form: 'Це Окса́на.' is 'This is Oksana.' The vocative is the same whether you say 'ти' or 'ви' to the person.

The ending depends on how the name ends, not on whether it belongs to a man or a woman. The main rules are:

- '-а' becomes '-о': 'Окса́на', 'Окса́но'.
- 'Мико́ла' is a man's name and a masculine noun, but it ends in '-а', so it follows the same rule: 'Мико́ло'.
- A hard consonant adds '-е': 'Тара́с', 'Тара́се'. A foreign name takes the vocative like any other: 'Сем', 'Се́ме'.
- '-й' becomes '-ю': 'Андрі́й', 'Андрі́ю'. The sound [j] of 'й' stays, and the letter 'ю' writes it together with the new vowel [u].
- '-я' after a consonant, in familiar names such as 'О́ля', the everyday form of 'О́льга', becomes '-ю': 'О́ля', 'О́лю'. The soft 'л' stays soft.
- '-я' after a vowel becomes '-є': 'Со́фія', 'Со́фіє'. The [j] stays and only the vowel changes, from [ɑ] to [ɛ].

These rules have limits. Some words take '-у': the word 'та́то' (dad), whose vocative is 'та́ту', and words ending in '-ич' or '-ик', such as the men's patronymics described below. Other names that end in 'г', 'к' or 'х', or in a soft consonant, follow patterns that later units teach as they appear. The stress stays on the same syllable in every name here; 'Се́ме' carries a stress mark only because it has two syllables where 'Сем' has one.

Formal address. To speak politely to a person you call 'ви', put a title before the vocative of the first name. 'Пан' (sir, Mr.) and 'па́ні' (madam, Ms.) are nouns, not pronouns, and they go with 'ви'. 'Пан' ends in a hard consonant, so its vocative is 'па́не', and both words change: 'па́не Андрі́ю'. 'Па́ні' never changes, so only the name does: 'па́ні Іри́но'. In everyday speech the title goes with a first name.

The most respectful address, used for teachers, older people and superiors at work, is the first name with the patronymic, a second name made from the father's first name. Both words are in the vocative. A woman's patronymic ends in '-івна' or '-ївна' and follows the '-а' rule: 'Іри́на Петрі́вна' is addressed 'Іри́но Петрі́вно'. A man's patronymic ends in '-ович' or '-йович' and takes '-у': 'Богда́н Іва́нович', whose father is named 'Іва́н', is addressed 'Богда́не Іва́новичу'.

grammar.title: Introductions: names, origin and nationality without 'is'
grammar.explanation:
In the present, Ukrainian leaves out 'is', 'am' and 'are', as unit 5 showed, so an introduction simply puts the words side by side: 'Я Сем.' is 'I am Sam', literally 'I Sam'. Three patterns cover a first conversation, and the first two are fixed formulas, learned whole now and explained fully in later units.

Saying your name. The usual formula is 'Мене́ зва́ти' with the name: 'Мене́ зва́ти Окса́на.' 'Зва́ти' is the infinitive 'to call', and 'мене́' is the form of 'я' used for the object of a verb, English 'me'. The sentence has no subject, so it says 'me to-call Oksana', in effect 'people call me Oksana'. The name stays in the nominative. To ask, use the object form of 'ти' or 'ви' instead of 'мене́', and start with 'як', 'how': 'Як тебе́ зва́ти?' to someone you call 'ти', 'Як вас зва́ти?' to someone you call 'ви'. English asks what your name is; Ukrainian asks how you are called. The object forms 'мене́', 'тебе́' and 'вас' belong to the accusative, which unit 10 teaches.

Saying where you are from. 'З' meaning 'from' is followed by the genitive, the case of origin, so the name of the place changes its ending: 'Кана́да' becomes 'з Кана́ди', 'Украї́на' becomes 'з Украї́ни', and 'Ки́їв' becomes 'з Ки́єва', with the change of 'ї' to 'є' from unit 5. Learn these three whole for now; unit 14 teaches the genitive. The question is 'Зві́дки ти?' or 'Зві́дки ви?', literally 'where-from you?', again with no verb.

Saying your nationality. A Ukrainian word for a nationality is a noun that names the person, with one word for a man and another for a woman, and it is written with a small letter, while the name of the country has a capital. English uses one adjective, 'Canadian', for both. So a man says 'Я кана́дець.' and a woman says 'Я кана́дка.', literally 'I Canadian-man' and 'I Canadian-woman'. The word for a man ends in '-ець' and the word for a woman in '-ка'. With 'ви' to one person, the word still matches that person: 'Ви кана́дець?' to a man, 'Ви кана́дка?' to a woman. For a group of men or a mixed group, the plural is 'украї́нці' or 'кана́дці'.

Questions and negatives work as unit 5 showed:

- A yes or no question is the statement said with rising intonation: 'Ти украї́нка?'
- 'Не' goes directly before the word it negates: 'Я не украї́нець.'

One point of writing: when a name is followed directly by a nationality, Ukrainian punctuation needs a dash between the two, so this course puts a pronoun in place of the name: 'Він украї́нець.'

grammar.title: Greetings and politeness: what the words literally say
grammar.explanation:
Greetings and polite phrases are fixed formulas: speakers use them whole, and the natural English equivalent often says something different from the words. Ask two questions of each one: what do the words literally say, and when is the formula used? The literal reading also shows the grammar inside each formula, and the table gives both answers.

The good wishes. 'До́брий' is the adjective 'good', and it agrees with its noun, as unit 5 showed. 'День' (day), 'ра́нок' (morning) and 'ве́чір' (evening) are masculine nouns, so all three greetings use the masculine 'до́брий'. 'Добра́ніч' is one word fused from 'до́бра', the feminine form of 'good', and the feminine noun 'ніч', night; it follows the preposition 'на', 'for'.

Verb forms used as formulas. Several of these words are forms of verbs, not interjections:

- 'Дя́кую' is the 'я' form of 'дя́кувати', 'to thank', so it says 'I thank'.
- 'Ви́бачте' and 'ви́бач' are imperatives, the command forms named in unit 6, of 'ви́бачити', 'to forgive'.
- 'Бува́йте' and 'бува́й' are imperatives of 'бува́ти', 'to be'.
- 'Будь' in 'будь ла́ска' is the imperative of 'бу́ти', 'to be', and 'ла́ска' is the noun 'kindness'.

An imperative ending in '-те' is for a person you call 'ви' or for a group, and the form without '-те' is for one person you call 'ти'. So the choice between 'ти' and 'ви' reaches even these small words: 'ви́бачте' to a stranger, 'ви́бач' to a friend. 'Будь ла́ска' is the exception: it never changes and is used with everyone. 'Приві́т' is not an interjection either: it is a masculine noun, 'greeting', used alone.

A sentence without a subject. 'Ду́же приє́мно' is literally 'very pleasant'. 'Приє́мно' is a predicative word: a word that makes up the whole predicate, the part of a sentence that says something, in a sentence that has no subject. English needs a subject and a verb, 'I am pleased' or 'it is nice'; Ukrainian says only 'pleasant'. Unit 10 brings more predicative words.

Asking how someone is. 'Як спра́ви?' is 'how affairs?', with no verb. The answer is the adverb 'до́бре', 'well', often with thanks and the question turned back: 'До́бре, дя́кую. А ти?'

rows: to one person you call 'ви', or a group
to one person you call 'ви', or a group

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: soft consonants, 'є' and 'ю' after a vowel, and 'в' as [w]
grammar.explanation:
Every word of this unit is read by the rules of units 1 to 4: each letter has its sound, the stress mark shows the stressed syllable, and unstressed vowels keep their quality, apart from the slight shift of unstressed 'е' toward 'и' and of unstressed 'и' toward 'е' that unit 4 described. The table collects the spellings that need attention, and these are the reasons for each:

- 'Приві́т' and 'спра́ви': 'в' before a vowel is [ʋ], between English 'v' and 'w'. Like 'б', 'п', 'м' and 'ф', it is only slightly softened before 'і', as unit 3 explained.
- 'Петрі́вна' and 'Петрі́вно': 'в' after a vowel and before a consonant ends a syllable, so it is [w], as in 'cow', and 'Петрі́вно' is [pɛtˈriwnɔ].
- 'Приє́мно' and 'Со́фіє': 'є' after a vowel is the two sounds [jɛ], so 'приє́мно' is [prɪˈjɛmnɔ].
- 'Дя́кую' and 'Андрі́ю': 'я' after the consonant 'д' makes it soft and gives the vowel [ɑ], and 'ю' after a vowel is [ju], so 'дя́кую' is [ˈdʲɑkuju].
- 'Кана́дець' and 'украї́нець': the soft sign makes the final 'ц' soft, [t͡sʲ], while the 'д' before 'е' stays hard. The 'ї' of 'украї́нець' and 'украї́нка' is always [ji].
- 'Будь': the soft sign softens 'д', and the voiced 'д' stays voiced at the end of the word, as unit 2 taught: [budʲ].
- 'Поба́чення': 'нн' is one long consonant, and 'я' makes it soft: [pɔˈbɑt͡ʃɛnʲːɑ].
- 'Зві́дки': the voiced 'д' stays voiced before 'к': [ˈzʋidkɪ].

A vowel can also drop out inside a word. The 'е' of '-ець' is there only when the word has no ending: when an ending is added, it drops out, so 'украї́нець' has the plural 'украї́нці' and 'кана́дець' has 'кана́дці'. The 'ц' stays soft, and the plural ending '-і' now shows it.

The alternation of unit 5 also appears in this unit's words. In a syllable closed by a consonant, 'о' becomes 'і' and 'є' becomes 'ї':

- 'Ки́їв' has 'ї' in its closed last syllable, and 'з Ки́єва' has 'є' in an open one.
- 'Петро́вич' and 'Петрі́вна' are built with one suffix: it has 'о' in 'Петро́вич', where the syllable 'тро' is open, and 'і' in 'Петрі́вна', where 'в' closes the syllable 'трів'.

rows: after a vowel, before a consonant
at the end of a word

culture.title: Names, patronymics and polite titles
culture.text:
A Ukrainian has three names: a first name, a patronymic and a family name. The patronymic is made from the father's first name. The daughter of a man named 'Петро́' has the patronymic 'Петрі́вна', and his son has 'Петро́вич'. Ukrainians address teachers, doctors, older neighbors and superiors at work by first name and patronymic, so a teacher named Iryna Petrivna hears 'Іри́но Петрі́вно' from her students every day. Among friends, classmates and young colleagues, the first name alone is normal.

The titles 'пан' and 'па́ні' are polite and warm at the same time. In everyday speech they go with a first name, and you hear them in shops, offices, cafés and between neighbors: 'па́не Андрі́ю', 'па́ні Гали́но'. For several decades of the twentieth century these titles were out of official use; since Ukraine became independent in 1991 they have returned and are now the normal polite titles.

The vocative is very much alive. You hear it in every greeting, on the phone and in text messages, and it is used for friends and strangers alike. Ukrainians value it as a sign of careful, good speech, and they appreciate a learner who uses it correctly.

Many first names have familiar forms used among family and friends. These forms are names in their own right and take the vocative too:

- 'О́ля', for 'О́льга', addressed as 'О́лю'
- 'Тара́сик', an affectionate form of 'Тара́с', addressed as 'Тара́сику', since names in '-ик' take '-у'

Use a familiar form only once the person uses it with you, or tells you to.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian phrases with the English
exercises.explanation: 'Приві́т' is only a hello, 'на добра́ніч' is only for bedtime, and 'до поба́чення' is the polite goodbye.

exercises.prompt: At two in the afternoon you meet your teacher, Iryna Petrivna. Which greeting do you use?
exercises.explanation: 'До́брий день' is the polite greeting from late morning until evening. 'Приві́т' is for people you call 'ти', and 'на добра́ніч' is said at bedtime.

exercises.prompt: Your little brother is going to bed. What do you say to him?
exercises.explanation: 'На добра́ніч' wishes someone a good night's sleep. 'До́брий ве́чір' is a hello for the evening, not a goodbye.
'Дя́кую' is 'thank you'; 'будь ла́ска' would be 'please'. 'До поба́чення' is 'goodbye'.
'Дя́кую' is the 'я' form of the verb 'дя́кувати', 'to thank'. 'Be kindness' is 'будь ла́ска'.

exercises.prompt: You are leaving, and you say goodbye to Oksana and Taras together. Which word do you use?
exercises.explanation: The imperative with '-те' is for a group or for a person you call 'ви'. 'Бува́й' is for one person you call 'ти'.
You are speaking to Oksana, so her name is in the vocative: '-а' becomes '-о'.
A name that ends in a hard consonant adds '-е' in the vocative.
'-й' becomes '-ю': the [j] stays and the ending [u] joins it in the letter 'ю'.
After a vowel, '-я' becomes '-є' in the vocative: the [j] stays and the vowel changes to [ɛ].

exercises.prompt: Mykola is a man, but the vocative of 'Мико́ла' is 'Мико́ло', like 'Окса́но'. Why?
choices: The vocative ending follows the ending of the name, not the sex of the person
Every man's name ends in '-о' in the vocative
exercises.explanation: 'Мико́ла' is a masculine noun, but it ends in '-а', and '-а' becomes '-о'. Men's names in a hard consonant add '-е' instead: 'Тара́се'.

exercises.prompt: In which sentence is Oksana the person spoken to?
exercises.explanation: 'Окса́но' is the vocative, so Oksana is being addressed. In the other two sentences her name is in the nominative because the speaker talks about her. Sam, who is talked about, stays in the nominative after 'це'.

exercises.prompt: You want to address Andrii, the café owner, formally. Which form of address do you use?
exercises.explanation: The title 'па́не' makes the address formal, and both words are in the vocative: 'пан' adds '-е' and 'Андрі́й' changes '-й' to '-ю'. The name alone is not formal, and 'приві́т' is for someone you call 'ти'.

exercises.hint_source: Nice to meet you, Ms. Iryna! (Іри́на)
exercises.explanation: 'Па́ні' never changes, but the name after it is in the vocative.
'Будь ла́ска', literally 'be kindness', is 'please'; 'будь' is the imperative of 'бу́ти'.
'Вона́' is 'she', and 'украї́нка' is the word for a Ukrainian woman.

exercises.hint_source: I am from Canada. I am Canadian. (a man speaking)
exercises.explanation: The speaker is a man, so the nationality word is the one for a man, ending in '-ець'.

exercises.prompt: A Canadian woman tells you her nationality. Which sentence does she say?
exercises.explanation: A nationality word names the person, so a woman uses the word in '-ка'. 'Кана́дець' is the word for a man.
'Зва́ти' is 'to call', and the question asks how you are called. 'How are you?' is 'Як спра́ви?' and 'Where are you from?' is 'Зві́дки ви?'.

choices: the form of 'я' used for an object, 'me'
exercises.explanation: The sentence has no subject: it says 'me to-call Olena'. 'Мене́' is the object form of 'я', and the name stays in the nominative.

exercises.prompt: Why is the 'є' of 'приє́мно' said [jɛ], with a 'y' sound?
exercises.explanation: After a vowel, as here after 'и', 'є' is the two sounds [jɛ]. After a consonant it would soften the consonant instead. The stress does not change the sound of the letter.

choices: Excuse me, are you from Canada?
Excuse me, are you from Kyiv?
Thank you, are you from Kyiv?
exercises.explanation: 'Ви́бачте' is 'excuse me', and 'з Ки́єва' is 'from Kyiv'.
The name after 'мене́ зва́ти' stays in the nominative; the vocative is only for the person spoken to.
Olena is the person spoken to, so her name is in the vocative. The question needs no verb.

exercises.prompt_source: Excuse me, are you Canadian? (to a man you do not know)
exercises.explanation: To a stranger you say 'ви', and 'ви́бачте' is the matching imperative. The nationality word matches the man you are speaking to.

exercises.hint_source: Nice to meet you, Iryna Petrivna.

exercises.explanation: 'Приві́т' suits a friend, and 'Оле́на' is in the vocative because you are speaking to her.

exercises.prompt_source: My name is Sam. I am from Canada.
answers: Мене́ зва́ти Сем. Я з Кана́ди.
exercises.explanation: Neither sentence has a verb for 'is' or 'am'. After 'з', 'Кана́да' becomes 'Кана́ди'.
Both the first name and the patronymic are in the vocative, and 'до поба́чення' is the polite goodbye.

exercises.prompt_source: She is not Canadian, she is Ukrainian.
exercises.explanation: 'Не' goes before the word it negates, and both nationality words are the forms for a woman.
